Nutrient deficiencies often appear first in leaves. Nitrogen deficiency causes uniform pale green or yellow older leaves, slow growth, and thin stems. Phosphorus deficiency can cause slow root development, dark green foliage, or purple coloring in cool conditions. Potassium deficiency commonly causes yellow or scorched leaf edges, weak stems, and poor drought tolerance. Confirm symptoms with a representative soil test because drought, disease, root damage, and compaction can look similar. Apply only the nutrient shown to be low, using the soil laboratory rate and a crop-appropriate product. Split nitrogen applications during active growth to reduce leaching. Place phosphorus near the root zone without touching seed or roots. Apply potassium according to soil texture and crop removal, especially in sandy fields. Recheck plant growth after two weeks and record the product, rate, date, and field response.

Soil pH controls how available nutrients are to crop roots. Test several root-zone samples from each uniform field area before applying an amendment; one handful may not represent the field. Acidic soils can usually be corrected gradually with agricultural lime, but the amount depends on soil texture, buffering capacity, and the target crop. Incorporate lime where practical and allow time for it to react. Alkaline soils may respond to elemental sulfur, organic matter, and improved drainage, but sulfur works slowly and should follow a laboratory recommendation. Do not use household acids or excessive amendments as quick fixes. Keep pH records and retest on a regular schedule. Organic matter supports nutrient cycling but does not instantly replace a pH correction plan. Select the target range for the crop, because a pH suitable for one crop may not be ideal for another.

Irrigation timing should match crop growth stage, soil texture, weather, and root depth. Water early in the morning when possible to reduce evaporation and give foliage time to dry. Wheat commonly needs reliable moisture around crown-root initiation, flowering, and grain filling. Rice uses managed flooding or saturated soil according to its growth stage; avoid uncontrolled standing water when drainage is poor. Maize needs particular attention around tasseling, silking, and grain development. Vegetables and fruiting crops need steady moisture during flowering and fruit set. Check soil moisture below the surface before watering instead of relying only on a dry top layer. Deep, less frequent irrigation is often better than shallow daily watering, but sandy soils may need smaller, more frequent applications. Stop or reduce irrigation after substantial rain, and improve drainage where water remains ponded.

Scout fields at least twice each week, especially after warm, humid, or windy weather. Early pest warnings include fresh holes, chewed leaf margins, leaf mines, sticky honeydew, webbing, curled leaves, wilted shoots, frass, and clusters of eggs or young larvae on leaf undersides. Inspect both healthy and affected plants and walk field borders as well as the center. Record the pest, location, crop stage, and number of affected plants so changes can be measured. Yellowing alone does not prove insect damage; nutrient deficiency, disease, drought, and root stress may cause similar symptoms. Remove heavily infested leaves when practical and protect beneficial insects. Use traps or scouting counts to decide whether treatment is justified. Identify the pest before selecting a crop-labeled product, follow the label, and rotate modes of action to reduce resistance.

Fertilizer timing should follow crop demand, root activity, rainfall risk, and soil test results instead of a fixed calendar alone. Apply phosphorus and potassium before planting or near the root zone when the test calls for them. Split nitrogen between planting, active vegetative growth, and the crop's highest-demand stage to reduce leaching and lodging. Avoid spreading fertilizer immediately before heavy rain or onto saturated soil. Keep granular fertilizer away from seed and stems unless the label allows contact. On sandy soils, smaller split applications are often more efficient than one large dose. Irrigate appropriately after application, but avoid runoff. Record product, rate, date, field, and crop stage. Compare plant color and growth with untreated strips when possible. A balanced nutrient plan is safer than correcting one suspected deficiency with an excessive amount.

Soil organic matter improves aggregation, water infiltration, nutrient cycling, and biological activity. Build it gradually by returning healthy crop residues, adding mature compost, using suitable manure, and planting cover crops that fit the local climate. Keep living roots or residue on the soil as long as practical and reduce unnecessary tillage, which can accelerate decomposition and erosion. Avoid applying unfinished compost or excessive manure because salts, weed seeds, and nutrient runoff can damage crops. Prevent compaction by limiting traffic on wet fields and maintaining drainage. Rotate crops so residues and root systems vary across seasons. Test organic matter periodically using the same sampling depth and locations so trends can be compared. Organic matter does not replace a soil test or immediately correct pH and nutrient shortages. Use measured amendments and allow several seasons for soil structure and water-holding improvements to become clear.

Crop rotation means growing different crop families in sequence on the same field. A useful rotation interrupts pest and disease life cycles, varies rooting depth, spreads labor and nutrient demand, and improves residue diversity. Include a legume such as chickpea, lentil, or mungbean when it suits the climate and market; legumes can contribute nitrogen through root symbiosis, but they do not supply unlimited nitrogen to the next crop. Avoid planting the same family repeatedly, such as cereal after cereal or a vegetable after a related vegetable, when shared pests and diseases are common. Pair deep-rooted and shallow-rooted crops to explore different soil layers. Keep records of crop, variety, planting date, inputs, weeds, pests, and yield. Design rotations around water availability and local sowing windows, and use cover crops where they will not exhaust stored moisture before the next cash crop.

Rainfall should guide sowing decisions, but one storm is not enough evidence of a safe planting window. Check the local forecast, recent rainfall, soil moisture below the surface, and the expected rainfall pattern for the next two weeks. For rainfed crops, sow after the soil has received enough steady moisture for germination and when heavy runoff is unlikely. Avoid sowing into a shallow wet layer over dry soil because seedlings may emerge unevenly and fail during the next dry period. Delay field traffic and planting when soil is sticky to prevent compaction. If heavy rain is forecast immediately after sowing, consider erosion risk, seed displacement, and drainage. Match the crop and variety to the reliable length of the local rainy season. Keep a backup plan for re-sowing, supplemental irrigation, or a shorter-duration crop when rainfall arrives late or stops early.

When a crop is stressed, diagnose the whole field before treating it. Compare symptoms on old and new leaves, inspect roots, note recent weather, and check irrigation uniformity, drainage, compaction, salinity, and herbicide exposure. Mark affected patches and photograph symptoms with the date and crop stage. Take a representative soil sample from the root zone, avoiding unusual spots such as manure piles or field edges. If a disease or pest is suspected, use a local agricultural laboratory or extension service for confirmation. Do not tank-mix several products without checking labels and compatibility. Small, targeted changes followed by a short recheck are safer than repeated broad applications. Keep a field log so recurring patterns can be linked to soil, weather, variety, and management decisions. Confirm fertilizer rates with a soil test, and follow all product safety, harvest interval, and protective equipment requirements.
